There is a good a compromise that for some reason is usually ignored by both parts.

GMOs are not inherently safe or dangerous, individual products can be.

If a GMO wants to enter the market it needs to be tested for safe consumption by an unbiased entity. If it's cleared, then it's ready to go. That's all there is to it.

It would be really great if these studies defined what tests make them "safe." Just a simple checklist of standard experiments that would be performed across the board and that could be replicated by anyone with the resources to do so.

With that said, and please accept my apologies because I can't find the link. There was a very interesting discussion about the complexity of testing GMOs. To put it simple, not all GMOs are the same (well, duh). Many, specially recent products, are basically small variations of existing crops. On the other hand, some products do come with important changes that need to be extensively tested (inclusion of new compounds) and then you have those that while don't exactly change dramatically the existing crops, they do change the way they are produced.

All the previous cases require different kinds of testing and an informed public that will understand the process.
